hello.note: Friendly and fine with anyone. Bom dia, good morning, is the usual greeting in shops

how-are-you.note: Polite, to anyone. Among friends: Tudo bem? (TOO-doo BAYNG)

im-well.note: A man says obrigado and a woman obrigada

good-morning.note: Until lunch. Then boa tarde (BOH-uh TARD), and after dark boa noite

good-night.note: Good evening as well as good night, both meeting and parting

goodbye.note: The everyday goodbye in Portugal. Tchau (chow) and até logo (uh-TEH LOH-goo), see you later, are common too

thank-you.note: Literally "obliged". A man says obrigado and a woman obrigada, whoever they thank

yes.note: People often answer by repeating the verb instead: Tem? Tenho! (do you have it? I have)

no.note: A nasal sound, like "now" said through the nose. Não, obrigado is no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Com licença, with your permission, to get past or get attention. Desculpe is sorry

my-name.note: Literally "I call myself". The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: Polite and the same for anyone: the Portuguese ask without a word for you

where-from.note: Literally "where is (he or she) from?", the polite way. Você, the everyday Brazilian you, can sound abrupt in Portugal, so leave it out

its-beautiful.note: For a place or a view. Que lindo! means how beautiful!

dont-understand.note: Literally "I don't perceive", the usual way in Portugal

speak-slowly.text: Pode falar mais devagar, por favor?
speak-slowly.say: POH-duh fuh-LAR mysh duh-vuh-GAR, poor fuh-VOR

repeat.note: Pode...? (POH-duh), can you...?, starts a polite request

speak-english.note: Many Portuguese speak good English, but they warm to anyone who tries Portuguese first

hundred.note: Cento (SEN-too) when more follows: cento e dez is 110

thousand.note: Prices are in euros: mil euros is 1000 €

hundred-thousand.note: Written 100 000 or 100.000, with a comma for decimals: 2,50 €

how-much.note: Point and say Quanto custa isto? (EESH-too), how much is this?

would-like.note: Literally "I wanted...", the polite way to order, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses um café (oong kuh-FEH), an espresso, as the example

i-want.note: More direct than queria. Add por favor. The audio uses este (AYSHT), this one, as the example

do-you-have.note: Literally "do you have...?", polite and the same for anyone. The audio uses água (AH-gwuh), water, as the example

just-looking.note: The same for a man or a woman

discount.note: Haggling is for markets and fairs (feiras), not shops

card.note: Cards are taken in most places, but some small cafés and shops want cash or have a minimum

bill.note: The bread, olives, and cheese put on the table (couvert) are charged if you eat them. Send them back if you don't want them

checkout-time.text: A que horas é o check-out?
checkout-time.say: uh kee OH-ruhz EH oo sheh-KOWT
checkout-time.note: The Portuguese use the English word

breakfast.note: Literally "the little lunch". In Brazil it is café da manhã

wifi.text: Qual é a palavra-passe do Wi-Fi?
wifi.say: kwahl EH uh puh-LAH-vruh-PASS doo wy-FY

toilet.text: Onde é a casa de banho?
toilet.say: OHND EH uh KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo
toilet.note: Literally "the bath house". Onde é...? (OHND EH) asks where anything is

taxi.note: Ride apps like Uber and Bolt are widely used in Lisbon and Porto

train.note: In Brazil it is trem. Trains are run by CP

bus.note: In Brazil it is ônibus. A tram is an elétrico

bus-station.note: For long-distance coaches, such as Rede Expressos. A bus stop is a paragem (puh-RAH-zhayng)

where-train-station.text: Onde é a estação de comboios?
where-train-station.say: OHND EH uh shtuh-SOWNG duh kohm-BOY-oosh

where-bus-station.text: Onde é a estação de autocarros?
where-bus-station.say: OHND EH uh shtuh-SOWNG duh ow-toh-KAH-hoosh

which-train.note: Para (PAH-ruh, often just pra) means to. The audio uses Sintra as the example
which-train.spoken: Qual é o comboio para Sintra?

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Porto as the example
two-tickets.spoken: Dois bilhetes para o Porto, por favor
two-tickets.filled: Dois bilhetes para o ⟦Porto⟧, por favor

trip-length.text: Quanto tempo demora a viagem até...?
trip-length.say: KWAHN-too TEM-poo duh-MOH-ruh uh vee-AH-zhayng uh-TEH ...
trip-length.note: The audio uses Porto as the example
trip-length.spoken: Quanto tempo demora a viagem até ao Porto?
trip-length.filled: Quanto tempo demora a viagem até ao ⟦Porto⟧?

delicious.note: Also Está ótimo! (shtah OH-tee-moo), it's great

allergic.note: Add the food: marisco (muh-REESH-koo) shellfish, frutos secos (FROO-toosh SAY-koosh) nuts, ovos (OH-voosh) eggs. The audio uses shellfish

love-dish.note: Literally "I loved this dish", the same for a man or a woman

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.text: Uma mesa para dois, por favor
table-for-two.say: OO-muh MAY-zuh PAH-ruh doysh, poor fuh-VOR
table-for-two.note: For more people: para três, 3, or para quatro, 4

menu.note: The prato do dia, dish of the day, is usually good value

beer.note: A small draught beer is an imperial (eeng-puh-ree-AHL) in Lisbon and a fino (FEE-noo) in Porto

coffee.note: An espresso, called a bica in Lisbon. A galão (guh-LOWNG) is a tall milky coffee

water.note: Com gás (kohng GAHSH) sparkling, sem gás (sayng GAHSH) still. Tap water is safe

hot.note: Hot, and hot weather. Spicy is picante

cold.note: Cold weather and cold food. A chilled drink is fresco (FRAYSH-koo)

help.note: Shout it. For police, ambulance, or fire, call 112

need-doctor.note: The same for a man or a woman. For an ambulance, call 112

pharmacy.note: Look for the green cross. At night, one farmácia de serviço in each area stays open, listed on every pharmacy's door
